extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in Herman Melville, Moby-Dick, and literary reception/textual history
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and descriptive criteria for how Moby-Dick was edited, censored, reviewed, sold, and later judged or adapted — covering censorship decisions, narrative/ stylistic criticisms, commercial metrics, and textual editions. Useful for assessing the book's historical reception, editorial changes, and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship: sexual matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual matters, including the sex life of whales and even Ishmael's worried anticipation of the nature of Queequeg's underwear, as well as allusions to fornication or harlots, and 'our hearts' honeymoon' were grounds for expurgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The British edition removed or altered passages judged sexual; some chapters or lines were excised or revised, and any of Melville's corrections to those passages were thereby lost. Example: many sexual references were suppressed while more indirect language (e.g., Chapter 95 'The Cassock') sometimes remained untouched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship: remarks belittling royalty / political criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks 'belittling royalty or implying a criticism of the British' were censored—this led to exclusion of material (for example, a complete chapter 25 'Postscript' on the use of sperm oil at coronations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers/editors in Britain removed passages judged offensive to monarchy or national sensibilities; such editorial choices altered the content available to readers and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative treatment of grammatical or stylistic anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived grammatical or stylistic anomalies were treated with 'a highly conservative interpretation of rules of "correctness".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors applied strict correctness norms when preparing the British edition, which resulted in alterations and the loss of some of Melville's marked corrections; this is an editorial criterion affecting textual fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative completeness: inclusion of the Epilogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The British edition omitted the 'Epilogue' (Ishmael's miraculous survival), producing a text in which the first-person narrator apparently did not survive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting material that explains narrative facts (like narrator survival) creates plausibility problems and prompted reviewers to object (e.g., asking how Ishmael could have communicated his notes). Complete texts that preserve such sections better preserve narrative coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title selection / marketability
rubrics_metrics.description: Late change of title to Moby-Dick because 'the new title will be a better selling title' — publishers and agents sought titles they judged more marketable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title choice is a commercial/editorial criterion: publishers may change titles to avoid confusion with other works and to improve sales prospects (example: Harper's earlier use of a similar title influenced the decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial performance: print runs, sales, price, and author earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative sales and earnings measures: British printing of 500 copies sold fewer than 300 in four months; Harper's first US printing was 2,915 copies (selling price $1.50); across years only a few thousand copies sold and Melville's earnings were modest (totaling $1,260 from the book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial metrics (number of copies printed, sold, price, subsequent printings, and earnings) are used to assess a book's immediate market success and publisher confidence; poor sales can affect a book's availability and long-term reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical authority / sophistication of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: British literary criticism was described as more sophisticated and developed, produced by 'cadres of brilliant literary people' and 'experienced critics and trenchant prose stylists', whereas American reviewing was often by less experienced newspaper staffers or amateur contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perceived expertise and cultural authority of reviewers shape reception; when critics of high status praise or condemn a work their opinions travel internationally and influence other markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise for imagination, philosophy, and poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers (especially in Britain) regarded The Whale / Moby‑Dick as 'a phenomenal literary work, a philosophical, metaphysical, and poetic romance' and lauded Melville's learning, dramatic ability, and 'prose poem' qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators may foreground philosophical depth, metaphysical scope, imaginative originality, and poetic prose as positive literary qualities; these attributes formed a major strand of favorable contemporary criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to extravagant digressions (narrative focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many critics regretted the extravagant digressions because they distracted from an otherwise interesting and even exciting narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive digressions that pull attention away from plot/character action are viewed negatively; maintaining narrative focus and appropriate pacing is an evaluative standard for fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to narrative conventions and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers objected to violations of narrative conventions (for example, introducing events the narrator could not possibly have known about) and questioned how the narrator could relate events if apparently drowned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics expect internal plausibility and that narrative devices not contravene basic verisimilitude unless authorial strategy justifies it; perceived breaches harm credibility and invite criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and language quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics said the style was sometimes 'disfigured by mad (rather than bad) English' or 'excessive' and 'too American', while others praised the style as original, witty, and poetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of prose encompasses clarity, idiom, national characteristics, and register; style may be praised for originality or criticized for excess and unconventional diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: realism vs. extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers found characters (especially Ahab) exaggerated and unrealistic; others argued that an extraordinary character was appropriate for the epic struggle with the white whale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative tension exists between expecting believable, psychologically consistent characters and accepting larger‑than‑life figures when thematically justified; criticism often hinges on whether characterization serves the work's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre coherence vs. essayistic/moralizing passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics condemned 'essayistic rhapsodizing and moralizing' that intruded upon the narrative, treating the book as 'three books rolled into one' (e.g., natural history, adventure, and philosophical essays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing documentary/essayistic material with fiction can be evaluated either as richness or as a flaw; coherence of genre and appropriate balancing of modes is an important critical criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and religious/professional sensibilities (irreverence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorter reviews mixed praise with reservations about 'irreverence and profane jesting'; some conservative readers objected to a perceived lack of reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone toward religion and sacred subjects affects reception among more conservative audiences; offensiveness or irreverence can provoke negative responses independent of aesthetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural legacy and adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's long list of adaptations (film, art, comics, readings) and influence on later authors demonstrates that 'different readers in different periods of popular culture have rewritten Moby‑Dick' making it a cultural icon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's adaptability across media and its influence on subsequent writers and artists are measures of long‑term cultural importance and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly/critical edition standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple critical/authoritative editions are listed (Norton Critical Edition, Northwestern‑Newberry critical text, Longman Critical Edition, etc.), often including introductions, explanatory notes, indexes, and contextual criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards for scholarly editions include accurate texts, editorial apparatus (notes, variants), contextual essays, and indices; such editions are judged by textual accuracy and the usefulness of their commentary for readers and scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical segmentation: chapter types and teaching suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters that are non‑narrative/descriptive are enumerated and said to constitute about one fifth of chapters — a structural fact relevant to teaching and curricular use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of the book's mix of narrative and non‑narrative chapters informs how instructors assign and frame readings; non‑narrative material may require different pedagogical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception measurement: what counts as a review
rubrics_metrics.description: The page counts 'some sixty reviews' in America, noting that the criterion for counting as a review was 'more than two lines of comment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring contemporary critical reception, explicit thresholds (e.g., minimum length) determine what is counted as a review versus a passing mention; such definitional choices affect perceptions of critical attention.
